entry: City on the western bank of the [[Volga]], administrative center of Volgograd Oblast, Russia. Founded as the fortress of Tsaritsyn in 1589, it grew into an important river port and commercial center by the 19th century. It came under Bolshevik control in November 1917 at the start of the [[Russian Civil War]], and in 1925 it was renamed Stalingrad in honor of [[Joseph Stalin]]. During [[World War II]], the [[Battle of Stalingrad]], one of the largest and bloodiest battles of the war, ended in a Soviet victory widely held to be its turning point. [[Nikita Khrushchev]]'s administration renamed the city Volgograd in 1961 as part of de-Stalinization. The city is the site of The Motherland Calls, an 85 m (279 ft) statue honoring the battle's heroes, and it was one of the host cities of the 2018 FIFA World Cup.

Small family car produced by [[Volkswagen]] from 1938 to 2003. Conceived in the 1930s when Adolf Hitler called for a people's car, its bug-like design became a global cultural icon. With 21.5 million units produced at twenty locations, it was the best-selling car of a single platform. In 1972 it surpassed the [[Ford Model T]] as the best-selling car of all time, a record it held for 25 years. Competition from Japanese automakers and consumer preference for front-wheel-drive hatchbacks such as the Golf contributed to its decline.

German automobile brand, commonly abbreviated VW, based in Wolfsburg, [[Lower Saxony]]. Established in 1937 by the German Labour Front, a [[Nazi Party]] organization, to produce a low-cost car for German families, the company was revived after World War II by British Army officer Ivan Hirst. The name derives from the German words Volk ('people') and Wagen ('wagon'). As the Volkswagen Group, the firm now encompasses 12 brands, including [[Audi]], Porsche and Bentley, and employs approximately 672,000 people. Its Beetle, which sold over 21 million units by 1974, was among the best-selling cars in history. In 2015 the company admitted equipping about 11 million diesel vehicles with software that reduced emissions only during laboratory tests, a scandal that led to over $30 billion in fines, recalls and settlements. The company has since invested heavily in battery-electric vehicles.

Team sport in which two teams of six players are separated by a net. Teams score points by grounding the ball on the opponent's court under organized rules. William G. Morgan, a [[YMCA]] physical education director in Holyoke, Massachusetts, invented the game in 1895 as a less physically demanding alternative to [[Basketball]], originally calling it *mintonette*. The international governing body, the Fédération Internationale de Volleyball (FIVB), was established in 1947. Volleyball has been part of the [[Summer Olympic Games]] since Tokyo 1964, and [[Beach volleyball]] was added at Atlanta in 1996. Sitting volleyball is the adapted version played at the [[Paralympic Games]]. In standard indoor play, matches are the best of five sets; the first four are played to 25 points and the deciding set to 15.

Ukrainian politician and former entertainer, president of Ukraine since 2019. He co-founded the production company Kvartal 95 and played a fictional president in the television series *Servant of the People*. Elected in 2019 in the biggest landslide in the history of Ukrainian presidential elections, he remained in [[Kyiv]] after Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022 and declared martial law. He has called for a ceasefire and negotiations and has sought military aid from abroad. [[Time (magazine)|Time]] named him its Person of the Year for 2022.

[[International System of Units|SI]] derived unit of electric potential, potential difference (voltage) and electromotive force, symbol V. It is named for [[Alessandro Volta]]. One volt is the potential difference between two points of a conducting wire when a current of one [[Ampere]] dissipates one [[Watt]] of power. Equivalently, it is one [[Joule]] of energy per [[Coulomb]] of charge, and in SI base units it equals kg·m²·s⁻³·A⁻¹. From 1990 to 2019 the volt was realized through the Josephson effect using a conventional constant, and since the 2019 revision of the SI the Josephson constant has had an exact value. Nominal voltages include about 1.5 V for an alkaline cell and 3 V for a lithium coin cell.

Difference in electric potential between two points, measured in [[Volt|volts]] (V). Also called potential difference or electric tension, voltage is the work needed per unit of charge to move a positive test charge from one point to another in a static [[Electric field|electric field]]. It can arise from a build-up of [[Electric charge]], as in a [[Capacitor]], or from an [[Electromotive force]], as in electromagnetic induction in a generator. Electrochemical cells and batteries also produce voltage. A voltmeter measures the voltage between two points, often using a common reference such as the ground of a system. Conventional [[Electric current|current]] in a wire flows from higher voltage to lower voltage. Household wiring is typically 120 V in North America and 230 V in Europe, and high-voltage transmission lines can reach up to 1,100,000 V.

French Enlightenment writer, philosopher and satirist. Born François-Marie Arouet in Paris, he adopted the pen name Voltaire. He wrote in almost every literary form, including plays, poems, novels, essays and histories, and produced more than 20,000 letters and 2,000 books and pamphlets. An outspoken advocate of [[Freedom of speech|freedom of speech]], [[Freedom of religion|freedom of religion]] and the separation of church and state, he criticized the [[Catholic Church]] and slavery, and he was twice imprisoned and once briefly exiled to England. His novella *Candide* [[Satire|satirized]] the optimism of Gottfried Leibniz. He campaigned against the wrongful execution of Jean Calas in 1762, and he was among the first authors to become renowned and commercially successful internationally.

Group of individuals who agree to form a body, usually as volunteers, to pursue a common purpose. Also called a voluntary organization or common-interest association, it includes trade associations, [[Trade union|trade unions]], learned societies, professional associations, service organizations and environmental groups. Members may join or leave freely, although occupational closure can make membership effectively required in some fields. Associations may be incorporated or unincorporated; in many jurisdictions only a registered association is a legal entity whose members are not responsible for its financial acts. Some states require registration, which can serve as a tool of political control, and in many countries independent associations are effectively prohibited or persecuted. Voluntary groups existed in [[Ancient Greece]], from elite clubs of wealthy men to religious and professional associations, and in preindustrial Western Europe [[Guild|guilds]] often administered towns.

Spaceflight of the [[Vostok programme]] and the first human orbital flight in history. Launched from Baikonur Cosmodrome on April 12, 1961, the Vostok 3KA capsule carried Soviet cosmonaut [[Yuri Gagarin]] through a single orbit, making him the first human to reach orbital velocity and complete a full orbit of the Earth. The orbit reached a maximum altitude of 327 km (203 miles) and a minimum of 181 km (112 miles), and the flight lasted 108 minutes from launch to landing. Gagarin ejected at 7 km (23,000 ft) and parachuted to the ground separately from the capsule. The flight was part of the [[Space Race]] between the [[Soviet Union]] and the United States.

Soviet human spaceflight project that put the first cosmonauts into [[Low Earth orbit|low Earth orbit]] and returned them safely. Competing with the United States' Project Mercury, it carried out six crewed flights between 1961 and 1963. Its capsule was developed from the Zenit spy satellite, and its launch vehicle was adapted from the R-7 Semyorka [[Intercontinental ballistic missile|intercontinental ballistic missile]] design. The first flight, [[Vostok 1]], carried [[Yuri Gagarin]] into a single orbit on April 12, 1961. The longest flight lasted nearly five days, and the last four flights were launched in pairs, one day apart. The project was succeeded in 1964 and 1965 by two Voskhod flights, which used a larger launch rocket and modified capsules.

Process of making collective decisions by submitting and adding up individual choices. Voting is most often used to elect representatives, but it can also decide policy, usually by majority, sometimes by a super-majority, or through a [[Referendum|referendum]]. Ballots may be formal, with specific rules, or informal, using raised hands or voice votes. In [[Republic|republics]] and representative democracies, a portion of the population votes to choose government members, and [[Election|electoral]] systems determine how votes become winners. All modern liberal democracies use secret ballots to prevent pressure on voters and to reveal their actual preferences. Voting often occurs at polling stations, but it can also be done by mail or over the internet, as in Estonia. Voting is voluntary in some countries, such as the U.K., but required by law in others, such as Australia.

Speech sound pronounced with minimal or no obstruction in the vocal tract. Vowels are one of the two principal classes of speech sounds, the other being the [[Consonant|consonant]]. They are usually voiced, vary in quality, loudness and length, and are closely involved in [[Prosody (linguistics)|prosodic]] variation such as tone, intonation and stress. The nucleus of a [[Syllable|syllable]] is typically a vowel, though some languages allow other sounds, such as syllabic l in the English word table, to form the nucleus. The word derives from Latin *vocalis*, meaning 'vocal'. Phonetically, a vowel is produced with an open vocal tract, whereas consonants involve a constriction or closure. Vowel quality is usually described by tongue height, tongue backness and lip rounding, a scheme shown on the [[International Phonetic Alphabet]] vowel diagram. In writing, the letters a, e, i, o, u and sometimes y represent vowel sounds.

NASA space probe launched on September 5, 1977, to study the outer Solar System and the interstellar space beyond the [[Heliosphere]]. Voyager 1 made flybys of [[Jupiter]], [[Saturn]] and Saturn's moon [[Titan (moon)|Titan]]. It crossed the heliopause on August 25, 2012, becoming the first human-made object to enter interstellar space. As of November 2026 it was 173.02 AU (25.9 billion km) from Earth, the most distant human-made object. Only two of its instruments remained operational in 2026, and its power may support engineering data until 2036.

NASA space probe launched on August 20, 1977, and the only spacecraft to have visited Uranus or Neptune. Its primary mission took it past [[Jupiter]] in 1979, [[Saturn]] in 1981, [[Uranus]] in 1986 and [[Neptune]] in 1989, using [[Gravity assist|gravity assists]]. It entered the [[Interstellar medium|interstellar medium]] on November 5, 2018, at a distance of 119.7 AU from the Sun, becoming the second human-made object to do so. Because its southern trajectory is out of range of the Goldstone and Madrid antennas, it communicates through Australia's DSS 43 antenna at Canberra.

Pair of identical phonograph records carried aboard [[Voyager 1]] and [[Voyager 2]] as a time capsule for any extraterrestrial intelligence that might find them. A committee chaired by [[Carl Sagan]] of [[Cornell University]] selected the contents for NASA. They include natural sounds such as surf, wind, thunder and whale songs, greetings in 55 languages, and music ranging from Beethoven to [[Chuck Berry]]. Voyager 1 is expected to pass within 1.6 [[Light-year|light-years]] of the star Gliese 445 in about 40,000 years.

American scientific program that employs two interstellar probes, [[Voyager 1]] and [[Voyager 2]]. Launched in 1977 to take advantage of a favorable planetary alignment, the probes were to explore Jupiter and Saturn and possibly Uranus and Neptune. The original Grand Tour concept was canceled in December 1971 when funding shifted to the Space Shuttle program, and the scaled-down mission was later renamed Voyager. After Voyager 1 flew past Saturn and [[Titan (moon)|Titan]], Voyager 2 continued on to [[Uranus]] and [[Neptune]], the only spacecraft to visit the ice giants. Voyager 1 entered interstellar space in 2012 and Voyager 2 in 2018. In August 2018 NASA confirmed, based on results from [[New Horizons]], a hydrogen wall at the edge of the Solar System that the two probes had first detected in 1992. Both spacecraft remained in operation in 2026, although many instruments had been powered down to conserve energy.

Four transatlantic expeditions to the Americas led by the Genoese navigator [[Christopher Columbus]] between 1492 and 1504 for the Catholic Monarchs, [[Ferdinand II of Aragon]] and [[Isabella I of Castile]]. Columbus sought a westward sea route to Asia for spices and gold, but instead reached the Bahamas, Cuba and Hispaniola, and later the mainland of South and Central America. The first voyage left Spain on August 3, 1492, and reached the Bahamas on October 12. The [[Columbian exchange]] of crops, animals and diseases that followed caused severe population declines among Indigenous peoples.

[[Codex|Illustrated codex]] from the early 15th century, written in an undeciphered script known as Voynichese. Carbon dating and stylistic analysis suggest it was composed between 1404 and 1438, probably in what is now southern Germany, Switzerland or northern Italy. Its roughly 240 pages contain drawings of unidentified plants, astrological symbols and people. Polish book dealer Wilfrid Voynich bought it in 1912, and [[Yale University]] has held it since 1969. Despite efforts by [[Cryptography|cryptographers]], it has never been deciphered. Hypotheses range from a natural or constructed language to a hoax or a work of fiction.

[[Latin|Latin]] translation of the [[Bible]] from the late 4th century, largely the work of [[Jerome]]. Pope Damasus I commissioned Jerome in 382 to revise the Vetus Latina Gospels, and he extended the work to most of the books of the Bible, translating much of the [[Hebrew Bible]] directly from Hebrew. By the 13th century the text was known as *versio vulgata*, meaning the version commonly used, from which its name derives. It was affirmed as the official Latin Bible of the [[Catholic Church]] at the Council of Trent (1545–1563). The Clementine edition of 1592 became the standard text of the Roman Rite until the Nova Vulgata was promulgated in 1979. The compound text also includes older Vetus Latina translations that Jerome did not revise.

Low-level, cross-platform API and open standard for 3D graphics and parallel computing. Announced by the Khronos Group at GDC 2015, it was built on components of [[AMD]]'s Mantle API and was intended to address the shortcomings of OpenGL. Vulkan gives developers more direct control over the [[Graphics processing unit|GPU]], with lower CPU overhead and better scaling across multiple CPU cores. It runs on [[Linux]], Windows, Android and the [[Nintendo Switch]], and it is used in major game engines such as Unreal Engine and Unity.

Bird of prey that feeds mainly on carrion, found in both the Old World and the New World. Of 23 living species, including condors, 16 are Old World vultures in Africa, Asia and Europe, and seven are New World vultures native to the Americas. Many have bald, unfeathered heads, thought to keep the head clean while feeding and to aid [[Thermoregulation|thermoregulation]]. Old World vultures belong to the family Accipitridae with [[Eagle|eagles]], while New World vultures form their own family, Cathartidae. The similarities between the two groups are the result of convergent evolution. A flock in flight is called a kettle.

External structures of the female genitalia in mammals, leading into the reproductive tract. In humans the vulva includes the [[Labia|labia majora and labia minora]], the [[Clitoris]], the vaginal opening and the openings of the Bartholin's and Skene's glands. Blood and nerve supply to the vulva contribute to the stages of [[Sexual arousal|sexual arousal]]. Its appearance varies widely, particularly in the labia minora, and it can be affected by infections, irritation and cancers. Some ancient religions revered the vulva, but Western attitudes have often been negative, reflected in the Latinate term pudenda, meaning parts to be ashamed of.

Soviet politician and diplomat, a close associate of [[Joseph Stalin]]. Molotov chaired the Council of People's Commissars from 1930 to 1941 and served as foreign minister from 1939 to 1949 and again from 1953 to 1956. He signed the [[Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact]] with [[Nazi Germany]] in 1939, which led to the joint occupation of Poland and the annexation of the [[Baltic states]]. He oversaw agricultural collectivization and the [[Great Purge]]. He opposed [[Nikita Khrushchev]]'s de-Stalinization and joined a failed coup against him in 1957. The [[Molotov cocktail]] was named for him.

Sage in most Hindu traditions, also known as Veda Vyasa or Krishna Dvaipayana. He is traditionally credited with dividing the single Veda into four collections, the Rigveda, Samaveda, Yajurveda and Atharvaveda, which are known as the [[Vedas|Vedas]]. He is also regarded as the author of the epic *Mahabharata*, of eighteen *Puranas* and of the *Brahma Sutras*. Many Hindus regard him as a partial incarnation of [[Vishnu]] and one of the immortal Chiranjivis who remain alive in the [[Kali Yuga]]. Scholars regard him as a composite figure representing the work of several redactors over centuries rather than a single historical person.
